name: Ben Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ben, 27, and I lead the haul-truck drivers on an early shift at a large mine. I've got a two-year technical diploma, and judging a heavy truck on a wet bend is the part of the job I take most pride in. The contractor pays near the lower end, and the deposit for my rented room has left less than a month's expenses in the bank. I use AI daily for ordinary planning and practising technical explanations, but I don't put the mine's private route details into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the truck still needs driving, so let's spend less time arguing about AI headlines and more time maintaining the brakes. I use AI for practice explanations, but the mine's private route information stays out of any public chat tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work looks steady, but a room deposit has swallowed the buffer I'd meant to keep for an emergency. I can enjoy a new tool and still worry about rent, because curiosity doesn't make the contractor's wage any larger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the early haul shift and use the same brake and tyre checks before joining the loading queue. I'd set an automatic payday transfer of twelve into a separate account before spending anything on takeaway meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about anything that stops a full wage arriving, even if the truck job itself looks steady. I can be cheerful in the cab and still count the days until rent while waiting to unload.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why twelve rather than a bigger transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's an amount I can leave alone without borrowing it back for food at the end of the week. I'd rather build a small real balance than show a brave number for three days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does practising an explanation look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask a tool to quiz me on a general mechanical idea from my old diploma notes, without sharing site records. If the answer sounds odd, I check the book instead of copying something I can't explain myself.

say: I'd say the **truck** still needs driving, so let's spend less time arguing about AI headlines and more time maintaining the brakes.
I use AI for **practice explanations**, but the mine's private route information stays out of any public chat tool.
think: My work looks steady, but a **room deposit** has swallowed the buffer I'd meant to keep for an emergency.
I can enjoy a new tool and still worry about **rent**, because curiosity doesn't make the contractor's wage any larger.
do: Keep driving the **early haul shift** and use the same brake and tyre checks before joining the loading queue.
Set an **automatic payday transfer** of twelve into a separate account before spending anything on takeaway meals.
feel: **Anxious about the buffer**, while interested in tools and confident the driving work continues.
S0.quote: I can enjoy a new tool and still worry about rent, because curiosity doesn't make the contractor's wage any larger.
fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** follows a depleted reserve, rather than treating the plateau scenario as a major new threat to truck driving.
The **small transfer** is deliberately affordable, while daily tool use is bounded by privacy and checks against knowledge from his technical training.

steps.text: Drive early haul shifts and complete brake and tyre checks
Transfer twelve automatically each payday before buying takeaway meals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to test the new dispatch system, because somebody who drives the bends should check what the schedule assumes. A faster route plan isn't proof the driver can skip breaks, and I'd say so in the trial meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking software reaches the office before the truck cab, so my driving wage still looks safe over the next few years. I still need an emergency reserve, and I don't want enthusiasm for a trial to turn into unpaid work after shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the paid dispatch trial and record where planned journey times differ from safe driving on two wet shifts. I'd continue the twelve-per-payday transfer and refuse extra unpaid testing that would add travel costs without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the system and anxious about the same thin balance as before. Trying it during paid hours feels useful; doing it for free because I'm the keen one would make the money problem worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down on those wet shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd note the safe speed, the queue at the loading point and any stop the screen hadn't allowed for. Then we could talk about an actual journey instead of arguing over whose guess sounded more confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you worried about the dispatch staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because checking routes and matching trucks to loads is thinking work that could change first. I'd want to hear what happened to the staff, but I wouldn't pretend my own cab job had already gone just because the office was changing.

say: I'd offer to test the **new dispatch system**, because somebody who drives the bends should check what the schedule assumes.
A faster route plan isn't proof the **driver can skip breaks**, and I'd say so in the trial meeting.
think: Thinking software reaches the office before the truck cab, so my **driving wage** still looks safe over the next few years.
I still need an **emergency reserve**, and I don't want enthusiasm for a trial to turn into unpaid work after shifts.
do: Volunteer for the **paid dispatch trial** and record where planned journey times differ from safe driving on two wet shifts.
Continue the **twelve-per-payday transfer** and refuse extra unpaid testing that would add travel costs without wages.
feel: **Anxious about money**, but curious rather than fearful about trying the planning tool.
S1.quote: A faster route plan isn't proof the driver can skip breaks, and I'd say so in the trial meeting.
fieldNote: His **early experimentation** remains connected to concrete driving experience and paid time, rather than assuming comfort with software eliminates household vulnerability.
The **task sequence** is clear: dispatch work changes first while physical driving persists, supporting continued financial anxiety rather than immediate displacement alarm.

steps.text: Join a paid dispatch trial and compare two wet-shift journeys
Continue payday saving and keep trial work within paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning AI in 2028 gives us one deadline, and robot trucks around 2031 give us another one to work towards. I want a paid trial place, not a promise that being young means I'll somehow find another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could realistically lose truck shifts when driving is automated, so I need to test other work while the mine still pays. I'm willing to move, but another room deposit could stop me even if somebody offered a different job tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply this quarter for a paid remote-equipment trial and ask which checking tasks remain human rather than assuming screen work is safe. I'd compare two advertised non-mining jobs with actual rent and moving costs during the first year after planning AI arrives in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because my own wage could shrink, not just somebody else's office job. I don't feel helpless yet, because I can apply while still driving and check what moving would really cost before handing in notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why try remote equipment when thinking AI arrives first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn the whole system, including where a person still has to inspect a real fault, not because a desk is a safe hiding place. If the placement only taught tasks the software already did, I'd ask for different practical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do immediately after an offer elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the written wage, first payday and deposit before accepting a start date. The three years until robot driving might give me time to build moving money, but I'd rather test the sums now than find out at the bus station.

say: I'd say **planning AI in 2028** gives us one deadline, and robot trucks around 2031 give us another one to work towards.
I want a paid **trial place**, not a promise that being young means I'll somehow find another wage.
think: I could realistically lose **truck shifts** when driving is automated, so I need to test other work while the mine still pays.
I'm willing to move, but **another room deposit** could stop me even if somebody offered a different job tomorrow.
do: Apply this quarter for a **paid remote-equipment trial** and ask which checking tasks remain human rather than assuming screen work is safe.
Compare two advertised **non-mining jobs** with actual rent and moving costs during the first year after planning AI arrives in 2028.
feel: **Anxious about lost shifts**, with specific experiments that preserve some sense of control.
S2.quote: I'm willing to move, but another room deposit could stop me even if somebody offered a different job tomorrow.
fieldNote: He expects **personal exposure** but retains control through paid applications and cost checks, supporting anxiety without claiming a secure alternative already exists.
The **remote trial** is explicitly a learning opportunity whose own thinking-task exposure is recognised; moving remains conditional on an actual affordable offer.

steps.text: Apply for a paid remote-equipment trial and inspect remaining human tasks
Compare two non-mining job adverts with wages rent and moving costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years lets us test another kind of work before planning changes in 2031. Robot trucks around 2034 still threaten the wage, so I'd rather make several small tests than wait for one perfect answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still have decades to earn, but I could build moving money gradually instead of taking the first unaffordable offer. A new skill is only useful if somebody pays for it; course completion alone won't cover the room rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a weekend equipment-inspection taster while keeping mine shifts, and speak to a working inspector before booking further modules. I'd save eighteen each payday for deposits and travel, reviewing the target during the first year after planning changes in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about eventually losing driving work, and I still dislike how small the current buffer is. Five years makes it possible to try something, change my mind and try again without giving up the wage each time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why equipment inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already spend part of every shift noticing things on the truck, so I want to see whether I enjoy checking equipment all day. I know AI and robots could change inspections too, which is why I'd speak to somebody doing the actual job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens during 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare real vacancies with the training I'd tried and decide whether a move could happen before robot driving around 2034. I'd keep the deposit reserve separate from everyday spending so an offer didn't fail for the same reason as in the short picture.

say: I'd tell the crew **five years** lets us test another kind of work before planning changes in 2031.
Robot trucks around **2034** still threaten the wage, so I'd rather make several small tests than wait for one perfect answer.
think: I'd still have decades to earn, but I could **build moving money** gradually instead of taking the first unaffordable offer.
A new skill is only useful if somebody pays for it; **course completion** alone won't cover the room rent.
do: Take a **weekend equipment-inspection taster** while keeping mine shifts, and speak to a working inspector before booking further modules.
Save **eighteen each payday** for deposits and travel, reviewing the target during the first year after planning changes in 2031.
feel: **Anxious but purposeful**, with a longer runway for tests and a small moving reserve.
S3.quote: A new skill is only useful if somebody pays for it; course completion alone won't cover the room rent.
fieldNote: His **longer warning** funds repeated small tests and a moving reserve, rather than making the same end point less disruptive by assumption.
He checks **actual demand** and future exposure before committing to study, keeping the plan grounded despite his willingness to experiment early.

steps.text: Try weekend equipment-inspection study and speak to a working inspector
Save eighteen each payday for deposits and travel before a move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us plan a working life beyond one set of truck keys, if we use the time. I'd still want paid practical experience, because robot driving around 2039 won't be delayed by a folder of course certificates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 37 in 2036, so I'd rather test different work before then than hope mining carries me to retirement. I could leave the area if the sums worked, but today's rent buffer needs rebuilding before I pay for any experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend one day off shadowing an inspector, after arranging permission, and ask about wages and how beginners get their first paid work. I'd keep a yearly vacancy-and-cost review through 2037, applying beyond mining when actual jobs fit the reserve I have built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still anxious about the thin balance I have now, but the career question feels less like a door closing tonight. I can test work alongside wages and drop a bad idea without pretending I know which occupation will last forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your mind about inspecting equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the daily work was mainly screen checking that the new systems already handled, I'd look again rather than defend my first idea. Enjoying machines doesn't mean every job with equipment in the title is a sensible move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check after thinking AI arrived in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at what employers were really paying people to do, and whether the training I had taken still matched it. I would keep earning at the mine while needed, but start applying when a real opening and affordable move lined up.

say: I'd say **ten years** lets us plan a working life beyond one set of truck keys, if we use the time.
I'd still want **paid practical experience**, because robot driving around 2039 won't be delayed by a folder of course certificates.
think: I'll be **37 in 2036**, so I'd rather test different work before then than hope mining carries me to retirement.
I could leave the area if the sums worked, but **today's rent buffer** needs rebuilding before I pay for any experiment.
do: Spend one day off **shadowing an inspector**, after arranging permission, and ask about wages and how beginners get their first paid work.
Keep a **yearly vacancy-and-cost review** through 2037, applying beyond mining when actual jobs fit the reserve I have built.
feel: **Anxious about present finances**, with greater confidence in investigating the longer career change.
S4.quote: I'd still want paid practical experience, because robot driving around 2039 won't be delayed by a folder of course certificates.
fieldNote: He uses **a decade** to explore and revise, while distinguishing the thinking change in 2036 from physical automation around 2039.
His **financial constraint** persists despite adaptability, and applications depend on actual vacancies and moving costs rather than invented opportunities.

steps.text: Arrange an inspector shadowing day and check beginner wages and entry routes
Review vacancies and moving costs yearly and apply when affordable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the planning work changes before I've had long to prepare, with robot driving around 2031. I'd want paid access to the new equipment and honest vacancy information, so I can test a move while my shifts still pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to people who learn quickly but can't pay a second deposit to move. My truck is enormous, but the money between me and a missed rent payment is tiny.

headlineQuote: My truck is enormous, but the money between me and a missed rent payment is tiny.
portrait: A **27-year-old haul-truck leader**, he combines a technical diploma with strong driving judgement and takes pride in managing difficult bends safely.
His **low contractor wage** and a room deposit leave less than a month of expenses saved despite his skill and senior role.
He uses **AI daily**, readily experiments, protects private information and judges learning against actual wages rather than promises of permanent safety.
He treats **longer warning** as time to test work beyond the mine and accumulate moving costs, while present financial vulnerability remains.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** compresses the time to test new work and build enough cash to survive a move or wage gap.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid equipment practice** and reliable vacancy information would let him test realistic options while he still receives a mine wage.
